doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

chapter: Learning from masters and guitar ideas
title: Playing with older musicians as a young player
summary: Johnson explains he hung around older men as a teenager; Woods adds the advice to play with better players, and Johnson calls each older master a school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah, Joe has the blues that he sings, he says, “You don’t love me, but then, I don’t even care. ‘Cause I’ll find a good girl somewhere.” So it seems to be that they are closely linked. And I don’t know, I think because you become a product of your environment so to speak, you can’t be in an environment and not be affected by it in some sort of way. So your age has a lot to do with it too. Because I was playing music that was a lot older and more mature than, you know 13 years old, 15 years old. So I hung around older guys all the time. I figured the young guys didn’t have nothing to teach me. They didn’t know any more than I did.
Well you know we’ve interviewed several musicians and every one of them has said, you know if you get a chance play with somebody that’s better than you. Jump in over your head.
So that you learn forms that you didn’t know, you learn chord changes you didn’t know, you learn voicings you didn’t know, you know? And you learn styles and maturity and how to caress the sound.

Well I, to me, that’s exactly true. To me I think that each guy is a school unto himself, each one of the older guys who I consider masters. And it’s oddly enough, a lot of them don’t even consider themselves masters. But us younger players we do, because they have reached a level of maturity and proficiency that we just aspire to reach.
